In 1921 Frederick Banting and his student Charles Best isolated insulin at the University of Toronto, in the lab of the Scottish physiologist John Macleod. Insulin is the hormone the pancreas makes to control sugar in the blood.

Before this, type 1 diabetes was a death sentence. Doctors could only put children on starvation diets that bought them a few months. In January 1922 a 14 year old boy in Toronto became the first person treated with insulin, and he lived. The biochemist James Collip helped purify the extract so it could be given safely.

  • In 1923 Banting and Macleod won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Banting shared his half with Best, and Macleod shared his with Collip.
  • The team sold the patent to the university for one dollar each, so that the drug could be made widely.
  • Factory production began within a couple of years, and millions of people with diabetes have lived on insulin since.

It was one of the first great medical breakthroughs to come out of Canada.
